MUQATIL:11:41-43/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:11:41-43/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:11:41-43/r3.claim: No one can protect from God's command of drowning; the exception is the believer whom God saves aboard the ark, and the wave separated Noah from his son.

MUQATIL:11:41-43/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:11:41-43/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:11:41-43/r4.claim: God was angry with Canaan because he thought the mountain could protect him from God and drowning.

FARRA:v2p15/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p15/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p15/r1.claim: من is accusative because the rescued person is the passive object مرحوم, unlike the active rescuer عاصم; the analogy ما لهم به من علم إلا اتباع الظن has a different semantic relation.

FARRA:v2p15/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p15/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p15/r2.claim: A nominative exception is possible only if عاصم is construed as meaning معصوم; Arabic can use an active form with passive sense, as in ماء دافق meaning مدفوق.

FARRA:v2p15/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p15/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p15/r3.claim: The poetry إلا اليعافير وإلا العيس permits raising the exception because wild animals count as the inhabitants of the land; this does not license raising من here.

AKHFASH:v1p383/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p383/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p383/r1.claim: سآوي is treated as a first-person form IV verb, explaining the word’s hamza and its reference to the speaker.

AKHFASH:v1p383/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p383/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p383/r2.claim: لا عاصم may mean there is no protector; alternatively it means no possessor of protection, with من رحم as a nominative substitute for العاصم.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p204#3/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p204#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p204#3/r1.claim: Yaʿṣimunī means protect or prevent me; lā ʿāṣima means there is no one protected today.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p204#3/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p204#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p204#3/r2.claim: The exception “except whom He has mercy on” parallels dāfiq in “gushing water,” meaning water that is poured.

TAB-FULL:v12p399/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r1.claim: In a report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, Noah loaded the animals onto the ark, beginning with the durra and ending with the donkey; Satan allegedly entered after Noah said a careless phrase inviting him aboard.

TAB-FULL:v12p399/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r2.claim: The report says the flood began as springs burst and heaven opened; after forty days and nights the ark rose on mountain-like waves, with iron nails in its planks.

TAB-FULL:v12p399/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r3.claim: Noah's son was secretly an unbeliever and assumed a mountain would shield him as mountains usually protected people from rain, but Noah said only those receiving God's mercy could escape.

TAB-FULL:v12p399/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r4.claim: Ascribed to the People of the Book, the water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains and destroyed all living things except Noah and those aboard, as well as the figure ʿUj ibn ʿUnuq in their account.

TAB-FULL:v12p399/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p399/r5.claim: The account dates the period from the flood's onset until the waters receded as six months and ten nights.

TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r1.claim: The son says he will go to a mountain for shelter; يعصمني means protects or prevents, like the waterskin tie that keeps water from escaping.

TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r2.claim: Al-Ṭabarī parses من as nominative: no one protects from God's decree except the one God shows mercy and saves, namely God; the sense is like saying no deliverer exists except God.

TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r3.speaker: بعض نحويي الكوفة
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r3.claim: Some Kufan grammarians parse من as accusative, the protected object, comparing it with the exception in 4:157; al-Ṭabarī rejects the reading because it requires عاصم to mean معصوم.

TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r4.speaker: بعض نحويي الكوفة
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r4.claim: The Kufan argument allows a passive sense in active-form participles, citing دافق, راضية, and the poet's الطاعم الكاسي for meaning poured, pleasing, and clothed.

TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r5.speaker: بعض نحويي البصرة
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r5.claim: Some Basran grammarians read إلا as لكن, or understand لا عاصم as no possessor of protection and من رحم as an appositive; al-Ṭabarī rejects these alternatives as unnecessary departures from ordinary Arabic.

TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p416#3/r6.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the common Arabic sense is clear without unusual grammar: only God can protect from His punishment, just as only God can deliver or provide food.

TAB-FULL:v12p419/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p419/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p419/r1.claim: A wave of water came between Noah and his son; the son drowned and became one of Noah's people destroyed by drowning.

ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r2.claim: Yaʿṣimunī means ‘protect me’ from being drowned by the water.

ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r3.claim: The exception may be separate from the preceding phrase: man is accusative, ‘except one whom God has mercy on,’ and ʿāṣim means someone possessing protection.

ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p54/r4.claim: Alternatively, man is nominative and means ‘no one protected except the one shown mercy’; rāḍiya can likewise mean ‘approved’ or ‘possessing approval.’

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r1.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r1.claim: The son thought a mountain would protect him from the flood.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r2.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq reports Noah's declaration that only one shown mercy can escape God's command.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r3.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r3.claim: Only the people aboard the Ark were saved.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r4.claim: Noah said no one could protect against God's command; God opened heaven and the wave intervened.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r5.speaker: القسم بن أبي مره
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r5.claim: The wave came between Noah and the mountain.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r6.claim: The flood stood fifteen heads above every mountain.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r7.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r7.claim: A woman raised her infant from her chest to her shoulders and then her hands as the water rose; God said he would have shown her mercy if anyone on earth merited it.

IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r8.speaker: عون بن أبي شراد
IBNABIHATIM:v6p2035/r8.claim: The water covered the mountains to a depth of eighty miles; the report then cites the command to earth to swallow the water.

NAHHAS:v2p284/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p284/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p284/r3.claim: The best reading makes من nominative and means only God protects from God's command.

SULAMI:v1p318#4/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p318#4/r1.speaker: author
SULAMI:v1p318#4/r1.claim: Only someone whom God guides to seek refuge in Him is protected by God from His command.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p473/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p473/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p473/r3.claim: Noah's son sought the mountain because he persisted in disbelief and rejected his father; one view identifies it as Mount Zayta.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p473/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p473/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p473/r4.claim: The exception may mean those on the ark whom God had mercy on or those Noah had mercy on by carrying them; la asim means no protected one, and God's command means drowning.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r1.claim: سآوي means that Noah's son intended to take refuge at a mountain to keep the water from drowning him.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r2.claim: عصمة means protection from harm; the mountain would keep the flood from drowning him.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r3.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r3.claim: لا عاصم means there is no preventer of God's punishment; إلا من رحم is a disconnected exception meaning that whoever God has mercy on is protected, with من in the accusative.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r4.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r4.claim: Al-Farrāʾ rejects nominative من for the disconnected-exception analysis: the protected person cannot be the one who protects.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r5.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r5.claim: عاصم may mean ذو عصمة, “one possessing protection”; then من is nominative and the sense is that none is protected except the one shown mercy.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r6.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r6.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows an active-form noun to carry passive meaning, comparing عاصم to ماء دافق (مدفوق), عيشة راضية (مرضية), and الطاعم الكاسي (المكسو).

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r7.speaker: علماء البصرة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r7.claim: Basran grammarians reject a general active-for-passive reading of ماء دافق; they analyze such forms as relational nouns meaning “possessing” the quality, so عاصم means protected by God.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r8.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427#2/r8.claim: The wave came between Noah's son and the mountain, and the son was among those drowned.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r1.speaker: أبو عثمان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r1.claim: Using alif in place of the possessive yāʾ is regular; he permits يا زيدا أقبل as an annexed form and connects it to the reading يا أبتَ.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r2.speaker: أبو عثمان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r2.claim: The poetry “وابأبا هما” supports the open form of the possessive ending.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r3.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r3.claim: In the kasra reading, the possessive yāʾ may have been dropped because it meets the sukūn of the rāʾ in أركب.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p427/r4.claim: The scene emphasizes the flood's enormity: mountain-like waves and water covering earth and all creatures except those God saved, yet Noah's son still seeks a mountain.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r4.claim: The son thought a mountain would shelter him and prevent him from drowning.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r5.claim: No one could block God's punishment that day; only those God had mercy on could be protected.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:41-43/r6.claim: A wave came between Noah's son and the mountain and drowned him.

JISHUMI:v5p3637/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r4.claim: Istʿiṣām is resisting a request to sin; its root means protection or prevention, as in the verse saying there is no protector from God's command.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r3.claim: “There is no protector from God’s command” is interpreted either with “whoever” nominative, making God the merciful protector, or accusative, meaning no one is protected except by God’s mercy, as in 69:21.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r4.claim: The flood rose forty cubits above the mountaintops; another report says fifteen cubits.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p178#2/r5.claim: An account tells of a mother repeatedly climbing higher with her child as the waters rose, lifting him above her head before they both drowned; even a mother’s love could not save them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r1.claim: Noah's son thought the flood was ordinary rain and water.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r2.claim: One analysis takes عاصم literally as the active participle; إلا من رحم means 'except God, the Merciful,' with من standing for God and in the nominative.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r3.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r3.claim: Another analysis treats the exception as disconnected: no protector exists, but one whom God has mercy on exists; this suits the meaning that denying a rescuer entails denying someone rescued, with من accusative, as in al-Nabigha's exception.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r4.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r4.claim: A further view takes عاصم as one possessing protection, effectively meaning protected; then the exception is regular and من is nominative. A raised exception cannot follow the line about a desolate place, since its gazelles and camels are truly companions whereas the saved son is no protector.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r5.claim: اليوم modifies من أمر الله or an understood 'good' that exists today, not عاصم, which would wrongly leave the word without tanwin; the syntactic rule is illustrated by لا أمرا يوم الجمعة لك versus لا أمر.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p174#3/r6.claim: بينهما means between Noah and his son, and the son was among those drowned.

TABRISI:11:40-43/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:40-43/r4.speaker: أبو علي
TABRISI:11:40-43/r4.claim: Abu Ali says kasra on the yā in يا بني is the correct reading: the root's deleted yā is restored in the diminutive, since long vowels cannot take inflectional movement and deleting it would erase the diminutive marker.

TABRISI:11:40-43/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:40-43/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:40-43/r5.claim: With diminutive, root, and possessive yā's together, the possessive yā may remain or be deleted while its kasra signals it; the latter matches يا عباد and is preferred.

TABRISI:11:40-43/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:40-43/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:40-43/r6.claim: A reader who opens the yā intends the possessive ending, replacing its kasra with fatḥa and its yā with alif, yielding يا بنيا.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r10.speaker: أبو مسلم
TABRISI:11:43#2/r10.claim: Abu Muslim reads Noah's invitation conditionally: believe in God, then board with us and abandon the unbelievers' religion.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r11.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:11:43#2/r11.claim: Under the other reading, Noah only tells his son not to remain with the unbelievers and drown with them.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43#2/r12.claim: The son expects a mountain to shelter him from the water.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r13.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43#2/r13.claim: Noah answers that none can ward off God's command and punishment that day except one shown mercy by God through faith, urging his son to believe.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r14.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43#2/r14.claim: Noah urged his son to board with them and not remain among the unbelievers.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r15.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43#2/r15.claim: The wave separated Noah from his son, who drowned.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43#2/r7.claim: Noah's son is named Canaan, though another report calls him Yam.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43#2/r8.claim: Being in a separate place means a geographically distinct area; alternatively it means estrangement from his father's religion or distance from the ark, and Noah called him because he thought he was Muslim.

TABRISI:11:43#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43#2/r9.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:11:43#2/r9.claim: Hasan says the son feigned agreement to his father, which explains Noah's invitation to him.

TABRISI:11:43/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43/r1.claim: The poetic phrases عيشة راضية and ماء دافق use active-looking forms with passive meanings, مرضية and مدفوق.

TABRISI:11:43/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43/r2.speaker: الحطيئة
TABRISI:11:43/r2.claim: Al-Hutay'a's line uses الطاعم الكاسي to mean someone fed and clothed, supporting the passive sense of the participles.

TABRISI:11:43/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:11:43/r3.claim: On either of the preceding grammatical analyses, the exception إلا من رحم is connected to what precedes.

TABRISI:11:43/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:11:43/r4.speaker: ابن كيسان
TABRISI:11:43/r4.claim: Ibn Kaysan says denying a protector also entails denying anyone protected; the exception for one God shows mercy to is therefore connected by meaning.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r1.claim: “I will resort” means I will turn to or return to a mountain; “protects me” means prevents me from drowning in the water.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r2.claim: Abu Salih transmits Ibn Abbas's reading of “no protector”: no one can prevent God's command today.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r3.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r3.claim: Ibn Qutayba takes “no protector” to mean no protected person, like adjectives describing something as flowing, secret, or sleeping.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r4.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj treats “except whom He showed mercy” as a disconnected exception: rather, whoever God has mercy on is protected.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r5.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r5.claim: Muqatil identifies those shown mercy as the people who boarded the ark.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r6.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Abu Salih, and Mujahid take “between them” to mean between Noah's son and the mountain he thought would protect him.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r7.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p110/r7.claim: Muqatil instead takes “between them” to mean between Noah and his son.

RAZI-FULL:v17p184#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p184#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p184#2/r4.claim: The son was Noah's biological son: the Qurʾān and Noah call him son, and turning these direct terms into metaphor lacks necessity; prophets can have unbelieving relatives.

RAZI-FULL:v17p184#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p184#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p184#2/r5.claim: Those retaining the literal reading explain Noah's call despite the earlier prayer against unbelievers in three ways: the son feigned faith, Noah hoped the terror would prompt belief, or paternal compassion and an earlier general statement left room for hope.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r1.speaker: حفص عن عاصم
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r1.claim: Hafs from ʿĀṣim reads يا بني with an open yāʾ throughout the Qurʾān; the other readers use kasra.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r2.speaker: أبو علي
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r2.claim: Abū ʿAlī prefers kasra: the diminutive and possessive form require the underlying yāʾ, and deleting the possessive yāʾ while retaining kasra signals it; the fatḥa reading uses a shortened alif form.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r3.claim: The son's plan to shelter on a mountain shows he remained obstinately disbelieving and rejected his father's warning.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r4.claim: Noah's statement that none protects except one shown mercy raises a grammatical question: how can the protected person be excepted from “no protector”? The author presents several solutions.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p185#2/r5.claim: The first solution connects to 11:41: God's mercy saves those aboard the ark from drowning.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r1.speaker: محمد بن علي الباقر
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r1.claim: A second view says the boy was Noah's wife's son, not his; al-Bāqir and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī are named, and Qatāda reports al-Ḥasan's defense from Noah's phrase “of my family.”

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r2.speaker: علي
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r2.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAlī takes the verb as referring to Noah's wife.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r3.speaker: محمد بن علي وعروة بن الزبير
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r3.claim: Muḥammad b. ʿAlī and ʿUrwa b. al-Zubayr are said to read ابنه with an open hāʾ, understanding “her son” with the alif omitted.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r4.speaker: قتادة
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r4.claim: Qatāda recounts asking al-Ḥasan about the apparent son; al-Ḥasan replied that Noah called him one of his family, not his son.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r5.claim: A third view says the boy was born illegitimately to Noah's wife; Rāzī calls it vile and contrary to prophetic dignity and the Qurʾān.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the wives' betrayal as Noah's wife calling him mad and Lot's wife directing people to his guests, not sexual infidelity.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r7.claim: Rāzī rejects the illegitimacy claim using 24:26 and 24:3, and concludes that the first view is correct.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r8.claim: The word معزل means a separated place, from the root of removal and distancing.

RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p185/r9.claim: Because the verse does not say what the son was apart from, commentators say he was away from the ark, apart from his family, or separate from disbelievers in a way Noah mistook for a desire to leave them.

RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r1.claim: The author calls the first reading excellent: God is the sole refuge, and refuge from God is refuge in God, as in the Prophet's prayer seeking refuge in God from Him.

RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r2.speaker: صاحب حل العقد
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r2.claim: The author of Ḥall al-ʿIqd supplies an implied object: no protector for anyone except the person God has shown mercy, like saying “we strike only Zayd.”

RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r3.claim: A third parsing treats عاصم as a possessor of protection, like “one possessing a spear” or “flowing water,” so the protected person can be excepted.

RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r4.claim: A fourth reading takes the exception to refer to God, whose mercy saves Noah and his party; help comes through God as life-giving is attributed to Jesus through his supplication.

RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r5.claim: A fifth reading makes the exception disconnected: rather, whoever God has shown mercy is protected, comparable to the disconnected exception in 4:157.

RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v17p186/r6.claim: The waves separated Noah from his son, ending their conversation, and the son drowned.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r11.claim: سآوي means I will retreat and join; يعصمني means it will protect me from drowning.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r12.claim: No protector can avert God's command on the day punishment has been decreed for unbelievers; عاصم is parsed as an absolute negation, though لا may also mean ليس.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r13.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r13.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes إلا من رحم as an exception outside the class: rather, whoever God has mercy on is protected.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:42-43/r14.claim: Another parse raises من and treats عاصم as passive معصوم; the passive-active pattern is supported by ماء دافق and cited poetry.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r1.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r1.claim: The preferred analysis makes من mean the merciful one: only God, the Merciful, can protect from His command; it avoids unusual senses for عاصم and إلا.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r2.claim: The wave came between Noah and his son, and the son was among those drowned.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r3.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r3.claim: One account says the son proudly rode a horse; after he reported the oven had overflowed, a huge wave swallowed him and his horse before he could join Noah.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r4.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r4.claim: Another account says he entered a glass house and sealed himself inside against the water, but drowned in his own waste.

QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r5.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:11:43-44/r5.claim: The mountain Noah's son sought is identified as Mount Sinai.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r1.claim: There is no protector from God's decree except God, or those whom He has shown mercy; only the believers in the ark have refuge, not someone climbing a mountain.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r2.claim: La asim may mean 'no possessor of protection,' as in 'a pleasing life'; alternatively the exception is disconnected: God will protect those He has shown mercy.

BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:11:43/r3.claim: The wave came between Noah and his son, or between the son and the mountain, and the son drowned.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r1.claim: The son says he will take refuge on a mountain, which he thinks will protect him from drowning.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r2.claim: 'No protector' may mean that none can protect from God's command except God; alternatively, no refuge from the flood exists except the place where God saved the believers, the Ark.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r3.claim: Alternatively, the exception is disconnected: the son has no refuge, but whoever God has mercy on is protected.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r4.claim: The wave separated either the son from the mountain or Noah from his son, and the son drowned; 'became' or 'was in God's knowledge' is possible.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p155#2/r5.claim: The disconnected-exception construction is compared with the verse saying they have no knowledge, only following conjecture.

QASHANI:11:41-43/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:41-43/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:11:41-43/r5.claim: The son's protective mountain signifies the brain, seat of intellect: relying on reason to escape matter cannot save him; only the one granted mercy through monotheism and religious law is safe.

QASHANI:11:41-43/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:11:41-43/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:11:41-43/r6.claim: The wave of egoic desire and bodily nature separates son from father and monotheism, drowning him in corporeal matter.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r4.claim: The son assumed the rain and springs were natural, explaining his habitual disbelief and distrust of Noah's warning; a report identifies his chosen mountain as Mount Zayta, which failed him.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r5.claim: The author keeps عاصم in its ordinary active sense and reads the exception as disconnected: no protector exists from God's command, but whoever God has mercy on is protected.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p158/r6.claim: Other grammatical readings make من رحم the merciful God, take عاصم as possessor of protection or as a passive participle meaning protected, or treat the exception as connected.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r1.claim: The poetry illustrates an active participle used passively; on two proposed parses, من denotes the protected person and the exception is connected, meaning there is no protector or protected person except one shown mercy.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari makes the exception connected by supplying an omitted noun: no refuge can protect from God's command except the refuge where the people shown mercy were saved, namely the ark.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r3.claim: The likely predicate of لا عاصم is omitted because it is understood from the son's claim; the author construes today as governed by an implied verb and rejects attaching it directly to the built noun لا عاصم.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r4.speaker: الحوفي، وابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r4.claim: They allow اليوم as predicate, with من أمر الله attached to it or to an implied predicate; Abu al-Baqa rejects a time adverb as predicate of a person-like noun, and likewise rejects it as an adjective.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r5.claim: A passive reading of رحم shows that the exception refers to the person who receives mercy rather than the one who gives it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p159/r6.claim: One account says Noah and his son were still speaking when a huge wave arrived; the boy rode a proud horse and was swallowed with it, while al-Farra says the wave came between the son and the mountain.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:43#2/r1.claim: A passive reading إلا من رحم supports interpreting من رحم in the common reading as the one shown mercy rather than the merciful one.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:43#2/r2.claim: اليوم and من أمر الله cannot depend on عاصم, individually or together, because that would make the noun long and inflected; al-Zajjaj's claim that its tanwin was merely lightened is rejected.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r1.claim: One view makes the exception disconnected: عاصم means a true protector, while من رحم is the person protected by God's mercy.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r2.claim: A second view takes من رحم to mean God Himself: no one protects except the Merciful.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r3.claim: A third view takes عاصم in the passive sense معصوم, supported by the poetic use of فاتنا for مفتونا; the exception is the person God protects.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r4.claim: A fourth view makes عاصم mean someone endowed with protection, which can describe either protector or protected; here it means protected.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats the exception as connected by supplying an omitted noun: only one refuge remains, the ark where those shown mercy were saved.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r6.claim: The best predicate for لا is omitted, estimated as موجود; Hufi and Ibn Atiyya instead allow اليوم, while Abu al-Baqa rejects a temporal predicate for an entity.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r7.speaker: الحوفي وابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r7.claim: Al-Hawfi and Ibn Atiyya allow اليوم to be the predicate of لا, with من أمر الله dependent on the implied stability.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r8.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r8.claim: Abu al-Baqa says a time adverb cannot predicate of an entity; من أمر الله should be the predicate, with اليوم modifying it.

SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r9.speaker: الحوفي
SAMIN-DURR:11:43/r9.claim: Al-Hawfi also suggests اليوم describes عاصم, but the author rejects this for the same reason that a time adverb cannot modify an entity here.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r1.claim: Noah's fourth son, named Yam, was an unbeliever; Noah urged him to board with the believers, but he trusted a mountain to shield him from the flood.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r2.claim: A claim that the son built a glass boat is an Israelite report whose reliability Ibn Kathir does not know; the Qur'an says only that he sought a mountain.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r3.claim: The son ignorantly believed the flood would not reach mountain peaks; Noah said no one could protect himself from God's decree except one shown mercy, with an alternative reading of asim as protected.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p323/r4.claim: The alternative takes asim as maʿsum, like words meaning something eaten or worn; the wave separated father and son, and the son drowned.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r1.claim: Al-Rummani transmits from Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak that Noah's son was Canaan, Noah's biological son.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r2.claim: The son was separate from his father in location and religion because he was an unbeliever; Noah tenderly calls him my son and urges him to board with the believers.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r3.claim: Noah's urgent plea shows prophetic compassion cannot soften hearts without God's permission, even amid terrifying signs; his son is so harsh he does not call Noah father.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r4.claim: The son says he will seek refuge on a mountain from the flood, but Noah answers that no mountain or other thing can protect anyone from God's decree except God's mercy, manifested through the ark or the one God has mercy upon.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p532/r5.claim: As the waters rise and overwhelm everything, Noah's son disobeys his father as he disobeyed God, goes to the mountain, cannot rejoin the ark, and drowns.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r1.claim: The wave separated Noah from his son, or the son from the mountain, and the son was among those drowned because he had not boarded with Noah.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r2.claim: Abu Hayyan says father and son were still exchanging words when a great wave suddenly swallowed the son and his horse, cutting him off from Noah.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r3.claim: The passage defines riding as mounting or being above something, running as passing swiftly or unobstructed, and a wave as a great raised mass of water.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p533/r4.claim: A mountain is a massive upright body rooted in earth, while protection means prevention from harm.

DURR-FULL:v4p432/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p432/r10.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v4p432/r10.claim: Ikrima glosses the exception to having no protector as meaning that only the people aboard the Ark would be saved.

DURR-FULL:v4p433/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p433/r1.speaker: القاسم بن أبي بزة
DURR-FULL:v4p433/r1.claim: Al-Qasim ibn Abi Bizza says the wave came between Noah's son and the mountain.

DURR-FULL:v4p433/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p433/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v4p433/r2.claim: The Prophet compares his household to Noah's Ark: whoever boards it is saved, while whoever stays behind drowns.

DURR-FULL:v4p433/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p433/r3.speaker: حميد بن هلال
DURR-FULL:v4p433/r3.claim: A worker who helped build the Ark chose his wage over Noah's offer of protection; when the flood came he tried to claim protection, but Noah said he had accepted the wage, and he drowned.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r1.claim: Noah's son plans to climb a mountain, mistakenly treating the divinely sent flood as ordinary waters from which elevation could protect him.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r2.claim: Noah's لا عاصم denies every possible protector, emphasizing that the mountain cannot save anyone from God's punishment; اليوم distinguishes this event from ordinary calamities where natural means can help.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r3.claim: Calling the flood أمر الله instead of repeating ماء magnifies the punishment, corrects the son's mistaken description, and establishes that only God's mercy can grant protection.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r4.claim: The strongest interpretation makes rescue by divine mercy the exception, redirecting Noah's concern for his son toward God as the true refuge.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p59/r5.claim: A second view treats عاصم as a rare relational form, so that the exception means no possessor of protection or protected person exists except one shown mercy; a passive reading supports this.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r1.claim: A third reading takes ʿāṣim literally and man raḥima as the one shown mercy: none protects from God’s decree, but one whom He pities is protected; the exception is disconnected.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r10.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r10.claim: He makes al-yawm accusative through an implied verb indicated by ʿāṣim, with min amr Allāh attached to that verb.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r11.speaker: الحوفي
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r11.claim: Al-Ḥūfī allows al-yawm and the prepositional phrase to attach to an omitted predicate, or al-yawm to modify ʿāṣim with that phrase as predicate.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r12.speaker: أبو البقاء
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r12.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ rejects a time adverb as predicate of a concrete noun; he makes min amr Allāh govern the noun and the prepositional phrase the predicate. Abū Ḥayyān also rejects the adverb as modifier.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r13.claim: The wave cut off Noah’s exchange with his son; a report says a huge wave arrived before their conversation ended and swallowed the son and his horse, while he rode proudly.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r14.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r14.claim: The verse itself only states that the wave intervened; Noah learned of his son’s drowning afterward.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r15.speaker: الفراء
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r15.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads ‘between them’ as between Noah’s son and the mountain; Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmit it from al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazza.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r2.claim: This disconnected exception is challenged as uncommon because its clause differs from the first in both affirmation and nominal versus verbal form.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r3.claim: A fourth reading makes ʿāṣim mean maʿṣūm and man raḥima mean the merciful; the disconnected exception means only the merciful can rescue whomever he wills.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r4.claim: The cited line uses fātin for one overcome, supporting ʿāṣim as the one protected.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r5.claim: A fifth reading supplies an omitted place and connects the exception: only the ark, place of the people shown mercy, protects; it fits the mountain refuge and ranks after the first reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r6.speaker: صاحب الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r6.claim: The sixth reading means no protected one exists except the place of those shown mercy; by metonymy, protecting the ship protects its occupants.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r7.claim: A seventh reading treats the exception as free: no person or place is protected except one whom God shows mercy.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r8.claim: Although some call the free-exception reading closest, al-Ālūsī chooses none over the first interpretation.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r9.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v12p60/r9.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says lā’s predicate is omitted as understood, ‘existent’; Hijazi speakers commonly omit it, while Tamim speakers require it.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r1.speaker: أبو السعود
ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r1.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd objects that the son’s drowning follows the wave separating him from Noah, since the mountain could not protect him even without a wave between him and the refuge.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r2.claim: A reply says the consequence need not be immediate, or that the son assumed the water would not reach him.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p61/r3.claim: The verse depicts unbelievers’ drowning as emphatically certain; kāna intensifies their being among the drowned rather than merely becoming so.

ELMALILI:11:43/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:11:43/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:11:43/r1.claim: This is not an ordinary flood from which customary means might rescue someone: it is a special divine command and tremendous punishment, from which neither a mountain nor anything else can save.

ELMALILI:11:43/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:11:43/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:11:43/r2.claim: Those excepted by God’s mercy are the people aboard the Ark.

ELMALILI:11:43/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:11:43/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:11:43/r3.claim: The well-known view is that the Flood was universal, though its universality does not extend to realms beyond the earth.

ELMALILI:11:43/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:11:43/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:11:43/r4.claim: On earth, universality must be measured over the inhabited regions; whether Noah was sent to all humanity or only a particular people is disputed, so a universal flood within his people’s region is certain and beyond it conjectural.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r1.claim: The son said this before the flood reached mountain peaks; āwī means to descend or take shelter, and its verbal noun is al-awy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r2.claim: “That will protect me from the water” can describe a high mountain or answer an implied question: the son thought the highest peaks would stay dry.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r3.claim: No protector exists against God's commanded flood except those whom He mercifully destined to survive; that mercy appeared in revelation of the ark and instructions.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r4.claim: The exception is from the implicit object of “protector,” since a protector necessarily implies someone protected.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r5.claim: Mawj names waves or masses of water rising through wind or inflow; the sea's turbulence also gives the word a metaphorical use for an agitated crowd.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r6.claim: The wave coming between Noah and his son conveys how quickly the flood rose during the attempt to escape.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p76#2/r7.claim: Saying the son was among the drowned concisely implies that the others Noah warned drowned too.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#12/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#12/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#12/r2.claim: The Torah includes a rainbow covenant, raven and dove reconnaissance, and specific ark dimensions and structure absent from the Qur'an.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#14/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#14/r3.speaker: بعض أهل السنة
TABATABAI:11:36-49#14/r3.claim: Some Sunnis argue for Noah's universal mission from the worldwide scope of the flood, Noah's prayer, the statement that his descendants survived, and a sound intercession report calling him the first messenger sent to the people of earth.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#15/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#15/r1.speaker: بعض أهل السنة
TABATABAI:11:36-49#15/r1.claim: Those denying Noah's universal mission interpret 'earth' as the homeland of his people, so his prayer and God's warning concern his own people and his surviving descendants rather than humanity everywhere.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r1.claim: Human society requires a divinely revealed religion and social law, so the first revealed law must have been universal rather than limited to one people.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r4.claim: Noah's mission was universal and his book, containing the law that resolves disputes, was the first revealed book with a sharia; the Book in 2:213 may mean his or the books of the great messengers.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r5.claim: Reports that Noah's invitation was not universal conflict with the Qur'an.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r6.speaker: الإمام الرضا
TABATABAI:11:36-49#18/r6.claim: A report from al-Riḍā says five messengers were the great possessors of resolve, each with a law and book and a mission universal to all other people, prophets and non-prophets.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r1.claim: Noah's universal mission entails a universal flood; this is the interpretive cue for verses that describe the punishment as covering the earth.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r2.claim: The command to take two of every animal kind aboard would be unnecessary for a flood confined to one region, supporting a worldwide flood.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r3.speaker: صاحب المنار
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r3.claim: Al-Manar reads Noah's descendants as the survivors relative to his people and says “earth” in his prayer can mean their homeland, as it does elsewhere in scripture.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r4.speaker: صاحب المنار
TABATABAI:11:36-49#19/r4.claim: Al-Manar says scriptural appearances and inherited traditions imply Noah's people were then the only humans; all died except his descendants, while the flood covered their inhabited land, unless dry land was then very small.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r1.speaker: صاحب المنار
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r1.claim: Al-Manar argues that marine fossils on mountain peaks can result from the formation of mountains in water, since a flood lasting days could not create them.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r2.speaker: صاحب المنار
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r2.claim: Al-Manar treats flood geography as historical rather than a Qur'anic doctrinal purpose: the text is not definitive, so contrary geology would not overturn a decisive verse.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects Al-Manar's reading as an unsupported restriction and answers that great waves could carry shells to high mountains and leave them there after the waters receded.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#20/r4.claim: The animal-pair command strongly indicates that the flood covered all dry lands, or nearly all of them, and that all people then alive drowned; no decisive proof overturns this Qur'anic appearance.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r1.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r1.claim: Alluvial lands were former channels for substantial streams and torrents, even where they are now dry.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r2.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r2.claim: The widespread deposits suggest that in the not-distant past torrents may have covered much of the earth's surface.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r3.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r3.claim: The scale and varying grain size of the sediments suggest flooding lasted or recurred over hundreds of years, with flows of varying strength.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r4.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r4.claim: Horizontal sediments can bend under strong lateral pressure over millions of years into folded mountain chains; intact horizontal strata are among the newest layers, dated here to at most ten to fifteen thousand years.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r5.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#21/r5.claim: New sediments expanded seas and separated former land connections, including Britain from Europe, Europe from Africa, Indonesia from Asia, and North America from northern Europe.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r1.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r1.claim: Internal earth movements redirected water: some coasts emerged even while water covered much of the land, as happened on the southern Khuzestan coast.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r2.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r2.claim: Geological evidence suggests unusually heavy rainfall at the start of the current human era, during the flood period, following extraordinary atmospheric changes.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r3.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r3.claim: Heat after an earlier cold period acted on residual northern ice, greatly increasing atmospheric vapor and producing unprecedented heavy rain.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r4.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r4.claim: Heavy rain on newly formed mountain ranges caused torrents to erode rock, excavate valleys, carry stones and sand downhill, and create new sediment layers.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r5.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r5.claim: Valley excavation opened underground water stores, releasing springs that joined rain torrents and increased destructive flooding across plains and mountains.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r6.speaker: الدكتور سحابي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r6.claim: The flood ended when finite underground reserves ran out and rain stopped, after which water drained into seas, lowlands, and emptied underground spaces.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#22/r7.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this geological reconstruction can fit the Qur'anic descriptions of rain pouring from heaven, the oven boiling, and the command for earth and sky to stop.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r1.speaker: بعض جرائد طهران
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r1.claim: A Tehran newspaper reported that American researchers guided by a Turkish military man found old ship-like wood fragments 1,400 feet up Mount Ararat, estimated at 2,500 BCE, for testing against traditions about Noah's ark.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r2.speaker: بعض الباحثين
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r2.claim: Some researchers reject Noah's reported age because human lifespans usually remain below roughly 100–120 years.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r3.speaker: بعض الباحثين
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r3.claim: One proposed reconciliation counts each ancient month as a year, making Noah's 950 years about eighty years minus ten months; the author calls this extremely far-fetched.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r4.speaker: الثعلبي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r4.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī calls Noah the longest-lived prophet and says his lifetime was a personal miracle: a thousand years without losing teeth or strength.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r5.claim: No evidence proves such a lifespan impossible; simpler early living conditions and fewer stresses and diseases could have allowed some ancient people to live hundreds of years.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#23/r6.claim: It is strange to object to Noah's age in scripture when the same scripture recounts many prophets' extraordinary miracles.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r1.claim: An objection asks why other animals deserved death in the flood if only Noah's people were guilty.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r2.claim: The author calls this objection weak: widespread death is not always punitive, as earthquakes, floods, epidemics, and plague often kill many, and God has wisdom in what He decrees.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r3.claim: Humans reason from observed causal laws toward distant conclusions and feel compelled to decide whether the universe has a cause, because the answer changes the meaning and prospects of human happiness.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r4.claim: Human nature first asks whether existence has a God, then intuitively affirms a creator who directs beings toward their perfection and receives them back after death.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#24/r5.claim: Because people know abstractions through sense and imagination, they tend to picture even a transcendent God in material, bodily terms.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r2.claim: People translate descriptions of God's transcendence and governance into a bodily image of a human-like ruler above the heavens, seated on a throne and directing the world.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the extant Torah explicitly presents God in this way and says humanity was created in God's image; the Gospels also appear to do so.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r4.claim: It is natural, especially for early people, to create a bodily image for a transcendent God; the Trinity can be pictured as a three-faced person, each face representing an attribute.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r5.claim: Recognizing a powerful creator naturally produces worshipful submission under the universal rule that the weak yield to the strong; conscious animals display the same pattern.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#25/r6.claim: Human submission appears in many relations; inward abasement before perceived power is one kind, and its bodily expression counts as worship regardless of who gives or receives it.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#26/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#26/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#26/r1.claim: This natural tendency to submit cannot be removed unless people learn that the being they thought powerful is actually their equal.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#26/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#26/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#26/r5.claim: Because people project abstractions materially and submit before overwhelming power, idolatry persists even in secular societies that honor statues and monuments.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r1.claim: Hundreds of millions still practice idolatry; the author infers that it began with statues memorializing great people, especially after their deaths.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r3.claim: Historical accounts say households in ancient Rome and Greece worshipped the family head and made an idol for the household after his death; some kings and notables were also worshipped.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r4.claim: The Qur'an mentions Nimrod, who disputed with Abraham, and Pharaoh as rulers worshipped by their peoples; Buddha and Brahmin figures also became idols.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#27/r5.claim: Worshipping statues of the dead suggests belief that their spirits survive death and become more powerful and influential after separation from matter.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r1.claim: People avoided depicting God directly because of His transcendence, instead worshipping supposed delegated rulers of particular parts of creation.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r2.claim: Communities chose deities for their interests, such as sea gods for coastal dwellers, valley gods for valley residents, and war gods for warriors.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r3.claim: Some chose attractive trees or stones as gods; Banū Ḥanīfa made an idol from dried curds and ate it during famine.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#28/r4.claim: Idol worship included blood-smearing and healing rites for diseased livestock, while sacred trees were left uncut and received offerings, vows, and gifts.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r1.claim: Other communities worshipped angels, jinn, fixed stars such as Sirius, or planets, hoping for benefits or fearing harm.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r2.claim: Idolaters usually made a wooden, stone, or metal image for a deity and gave it a human or animal form, even when the supposed god was a star or abstract power.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#29/r3.claim: They used idols as accessible representations when a god was invisible or too mobile for direct ritual attention, imagining the image expressed its attributes.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#3/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#3/r5.speaker: علي بن موسى الرضا
TABATABAI:11:36-49#3/r5.claim: Al-Rida says Noah's son was excluded from his family because he opposed Noah's religion, while Noah counted those who followed him as family; the son was biologically his, contrary to readings making him his wife's child.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#3/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#3/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#3/r6.claim: Al-Tabataba'i connects the saved 'family' with all rescued companions in 21:76, and says the two reported recitations were interpreted to support an illegitimate-son reading; the Qur'an's wording does not support it, and the Torah is silent about the drowned son.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#34/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#34/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#34/r7.claim: Before Islam, most Arabs were nomadic; settled Yemen also retained a nomadic outlook and borrowed customs and religious practices from neighboring powers.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r1.claim: The Qur'an depicts early Arabs, including ʿĀd, Iram, Thamud, Midian, and Saba, as idolaters.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r3.claim: Some Bedouins adopted Judaism through contact with Hijazi Jews, while Christianity and Magianism spread in other parts of Arabia.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r4.claim: After recovering at a Syrian hot spring, ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy copied local idol worship, brought Hubal to Mecca, and reintroduced idols after the people of Abraham had been called hanifs.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#35/r5.claim: Because Jews, Christians, Magians, and idolaters all honored the Kaaba, travelers carried sanctuary stones away, set them up, and circled them, helping idolatry spread.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#36/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#36/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#36/r5.claim: Arab custom mixed Abrahamic practices such as circumcision and pilgrimage with idolatry, naked circumambulation, associating partners in the talbiya, and invented taboos and divination rites.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r1.claim: Muhammad called his people to monotheism through wisdom and good exhortation; they mocked and persecuted believers, forcing emigration, then plotted to kill him before his migration to Medina.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r2.claim: After the conquest of Mecca, Muhammad cleared the sanctuary of idols; Ali threw Hubal from the Kaaba roof, and reports say it was buried at the mosque threshold.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r3.claim: Islam removes idolatry at its roots: only God exists independently, while all else begins from and returns to Him and depends on Him; assigning others independence is shirk.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r4.claim: Islam cultivates reliance, trust, love, and action for God alone, and forbids dependence on others, prostration to others, images, unauthorized obedience, innovation, and following Satan.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم وأئمة أهل البيت عليهم السلام
TABATABAI:11:36-49#37/r5.claim: Reports distinguish manifest and hidden shirk and many degrees; only the sincere are wholly free, and shirk can be subtler than an ant walking on a dark stone at night.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r1.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r1.claim: The sound heart in 26:88–89 meets God with no one else in it; a heart containing shirk or doubt is lost.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r2.claim: Renunciation of worldly attachments is meant to free hearts for the afterlife.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r3.claim: A report distinguishes worship for Paradise as hired labor, worship from fear of Hell as servitude, and worship from love of God as the worship of the noble.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#38/r4.claim: The Prophet's program called People of the Book to worship God alone and reject partners or human lords; the Qur'an also condemns religious excess and following misguided desires.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r1.claim: The Prophet enacted monotheism socially by applying law equally, rejecting inherited rank, and treating people alike except for piety before God.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r2.claim: He lived like ordinary people and discouraged displays of wealth or power that humiliated the poor and weak.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r3.claim: Brahmanism, Buddhism, and Sabianism are described as teaching endless cycles of worlds, with new bodies after death assigned according to deeds and acquired character.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r4.claim: Good deeds lead to a happy rebirth, while earthly attachment leads to a miserable body and suffering; knowing Brahman and uniting with it ends rebirth.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r5.claim: Religious duty is to believe in Brahman, worship, and cultivate virtue; if union is not attained, good conduct brings happiness in a later life.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r6.claim: Because Brahman is considered too transcendent to approach directly, worshipers seek its favor through intermediaries such as angels, jinn, perfected souls, and beings called its spouses or children.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#39/r7.claim: In this account, jinn are worshiped from fear, while other divine intermediaries are worshiped from hope of mercy and fear of displeasure.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r1.claim: The author rejects the argument that Noah's son could not be his biological child because Noah invoked the promise to save his family: the promise did not say all his descendants would be saved.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر محمد بن علي
TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r2.claim: Al-Baqir is reported to explain 'his son' as a Tayy dialect expression for a wife's son, even though the author ultimately relies on al-Rida's report that he was Noah's biological son.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r3.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABATABAI:11:36-49#4/r3.claim: Al-Sadiq likewise explains that Tayy speakers call a wife's son her son; al-Baqir is also reported as saying Noah did not know the boy's true status when he called him 'my son.'

TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r1.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues that the Upanishads contain a higher monotheism than popular Brahmanism: absolute God has life, knowledge, and power without material limits, peer, birth, or offspring.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r2.claim: He says the Upanishads affirm worship of God alone, resurrection, and postmortem reward and punishment compatible with the intermediate realm, without support for idols or reincarnation.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r3.claim: He suggests these truths were first disclosed by a few spiritually guided people in symbolic language, then became the basis of a popular religion ordinary people could not fully grasp.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#40/r4.claim: Making an exclusive, elite religion the public way of life conflicts with humans' innate social nature and separates people from one another.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r1.claim: Revelation, spiritual unveiling, and reason are three routes of knowledge; reason is the broadest and most necessary for worldly life, even for prophets and mystics.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r2.claim: Neglecting reason imposes blind imitation across belief, morals, and conduct and undermines human dignity; the author also links idolatrous religious orders with social enslavement.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r3.claim: Religions that profess one God can still fall into worshipful shirk; the author says Buddhism and Sabianism show this plainly.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r4.claim: The Magians profess Ahura Mazda as God but revere Yazdan, Ahriman, angels, the sun, and fire; the author links their social stratification to corruption of original religion.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r5.claim: A report says the Magians once had a prophet whom they killed and a scripture they burned.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r6.claim: The Qur'an recounts Jewish alteration of scripture and deification of scholars; the author directs readers to an earlier treatment of Christian doctrinal and historical departures.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#41/r7.claim: Islam repairs these errors by expressing high truths in plain language ordinary minds can absorb, while allowing spiritually mature people to access their full depth.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r1.claim: The Prophet says prophets were instructed to address people according to their capacity.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r2.claim: Islam denies independent existence or attributes to anything besides God, describes divine qualities without likening them to human qualities, and requires beliefs to rest on knowledge and rational proof.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r3.claim: This approach makes religion equally available to ordinary and learned people, uses sound reason, and brings social classes closer without privileging one over another.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#42/r4.claim: An objection says intercession, supplication by prophets' rank, grave visits, and seeking blessing from relics are shirk because idolaters likewise claimed their idols interceded.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r1.claim: He rejects the argument: created causes can have effects, but only God acts independently; denying every secondary effect would destroy causality and arguments for monotheism.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r2.claim: The Qur'an authorizes intercession by those God approves and directs believers to seek a way to Him; honoring prophets and saints as signs is a means if they are not worshiped independently.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:11:36-49#43/r3.claim: Worshiping an intermediary for its independent favor differs from worshiping God alone while seeking intercession; the Kaaba and Black Stone likewise provide direction, not objects of worship.

TABATABAI:11:36-49#7/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
